doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Veterans, early discharges and the rule against war stories
summary: Classmates discharged early, John Fell's typed release, the end of the 'crazy mixed up years,' and veterans who never spoke about combat.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Yeah they weren’t doing any of that stuff. But in my class you had a lot of guys who had got drafted right at the end of the war, as we were saying, and had been serving, maybe they served for a year or for six months, whatever, and were released because they were discharging everybody. This was 1946, they were discharging everybody, get them out, because our government didn’t want to pay for their —
Oh I didn’t know that, that you might have gone in for just a year and then got —

They were disbanding the Army, get rid of them, get rid of them, and send everybody home. So people were getting out and I remember John Fell, who was the clarinet player in our band, John was in a situation like this, he’d only been in for a while but he was a very bright guy and he could type and — which was not so usual in those days — and he was a clerk somewhere in the Army, and the order came through that if you could go back to college immediately you could be discharged. So he pulled out a form and typed it up and put it in and went home. And so guys were getting out. So my freshman class was filled with these guys who had only been in for a short period of time.
They called that the “crazy mixed up years” didn’t they?

Well no, that was the years just before us. Because by the time 1946, the war is over, we’re coming into a peacetime situation, the college has increased in size — it was the years before when people were coming and going and they would come for a year or come for a year and a half, come for six months, get drafted, and then come back. And that was the crazy mixed up years. Ours had started back to normality — and the word is not normalcy — normality again, and we had sort of it was back to normal, except we had all these guys who had seen it all, and there was a big rule that you didn’t tell war stories. There was a whole thing about that, you did not.

I’ve known a lot of — over the course of my life obviously — a lot of guys my age more or less who were combat vets. They don’t talk about it. They just don’t. It’s too difficult in many ways. You don’t want to show off, that was another thing. And I played jazz with a guy called Flip Don Phillips who died recently. And Don I knew for twenty years. And he was in combat in France and I never knew anything about that until the last couple of years of his life. He just never talked about it. So that was the situation there. Now I’ll segue into jazz. I got up to Hamilton at that time when you were admitted they sent you a form which was sent around to the fraternities and, I don’t know, you put down whatever you were that might appeal to the fraternities.
